title: Overlapping daemon starts can leave the first child running beside the second
body:
## Summary
`daemon::start` is not serialised, so two `daemon_restart` calls that overlap can each spawn a daemon, and the second overwrites the first's handle without killing it.

## Description
`start` (apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/daemon.rs:770) runs `state.shutdown()`, bumps the generation, spawns, and only then stores the child with `*state.locked_child() = Some(child)` (daemon.rs:861). Nothing holds a lock across those steps, and `daemon_restart` is an async command (daemon.rs:1070), so two invocations run on two runtime threads. If both pass `shutdown()` before either stores its child, the second store drops the first `Child` without `kill_tree`: that daemon keeps its port and the same brain directory until the shell exits (the Windows job object reaps it then; elsewhere nothing does). The panel serialises restarts per window (apps/desktop/src/stores/daemon.ts:144 `enqueue`), but the companion window and Main each have their own store and both can restart (apps/desktop/src/companion/live.tsx:385, apps/desktop/src/modules/setup/index.ts:71). Technique subprocess-lifecycle (creation names its reaper). Fixed looks like: one start at a time (a `starting` mutex held across shutdown-spawn-store), and storing a child kills any child it replaces.

## Flow
- Main's Setup restarts on its engine while the companion's engine picker restarts on another, within the same ~150 ms shutdown grace
- both `start` calls shut down nothing new, both spawn, the later `*locked_child() = Some(child)` drops the earlier handle
- two `athena serve` processes now share `<app data>/brain`; the status describes only the second

## Expected impact
Anyone who changes engine from both windows at once; measured as daemons alive after two overlapping restarts (2 predicted today, 1 after). Could break: a lock held across `start` makes a second restart wait up to the shutdown grace plus a taskkill.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience - one daemon per shell even under overlapping restarts
Before: simulation - the interleaving above walked on daemon.rs:770-865; not reproduced (needs two concurrent `start` calls on a live AppHandle)
After: predicted 1 daemon; the replaced child killed
Method: simulation - a probe needs an AppHandle or a refactor that lets a test install two children
Result: better
Gate: none
instrument: daemon.rs unit test: extract `Daemon::install(child)` that kills and reaps any child it replaces; spawn two real `cmd /c ping -n 30` children, install both, assert the first has exited within 1 s (red today: the first keeps running).

title: A tab opens any URL scheme the parser accepts, bridge and hands injected
body:
## Summary
`tabs::create` and `tabs::navigate` accept any URL `Url::parse` accepts (`file:`, `data:`, custom schemes) and build a page webview with `inject.js`, the relay and `hands.js` in it; nothing on the native side bounds what a tab may open.

## Description
apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/tabs.rs:193 and :291 parse the string and nothing else; the URL comes from the presentation layer (`tabs_create`, apps/desktop/src/stores/tabs.ts:38, the playbook portal at apps/desktop/src/modules/playbooks/index.ts:47) or from argv (`start_url`, apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs:286). A `file:///C:/Users/...` page then holds the hands: `origin_of` answers "" for it (tabs.rs:178), so it is never a trusted origin and every hand is GATED, which is the mitigation in place. Registry native-shell-integration, technique native-side-owns-the-target-set, rule two: where a target must cross, the native side owns a positive allow-list (http, https, and whatever local scheme the product means to support). Which schemes a tab may open is a product decision (a local HTML report, `about:blank`), so this card is the decision, not the code.

## Flow
- the address field or a playbook hands `file:///...` (or a `data:` URL) to `tabs_create`
- tabs.rs builds a page webview for it with the three initialization scripts
- the model can be offered page_read on a local file, behind a card

## Expected impact
Defence in depth for the user's own files; measured as schemes `tabs_create` accepts (unbounded today, an allow-list after). Could break: any workflow that opens local HTML in a tab.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality - the native side bounds what a tab may open
Before: probe by reading - tabs.rs:193 `Url::parse(url)` is the only check; schemes accepted: any
After: an allow-list the owner chooses
Method: simulation - the harm is gated today by origin_of's empty origin, so no reproduced exposure; the open question is which schemes to allow
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: policy-tighten

title: The hands' own prose still counts nine hands, eight of them the page's
body:
## Summary
hands.js, hands.test.ts and hands.rs describe the catalogue as nine hands with one shell hand, but `tabs_read` made it ten with two shell hands and hands.js holds eight.

## Description
apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/hands.js:2 "The nine generic hands" (the file declares eight in `FLAGS`, hands.js:782); apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/hands.test.ts:4 the same; apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/hands.rs:52-55 "Eight of the nine are the page's ... The ninth is the shell's" and hands.rs:1280 a test variable `ninth` for SCREENSHOT, while `HANDS` holds ten and `eight_hands_are_the_pages_and_two_are_the_shells` pins two shell hands. Prose that states the shape of a two-language capability is what a reader uses to decide where a new hand goes. Fixed looks like: counts that match the tables, and one test in hands.test.ts that reads the script header's count against `FLAGS`.

## Flow
- a contributor reads hands.js's header, adds a page hand and believes nine is the total
- the Rust module says the shell answers one hand while `call` dispatches two

## Expected impact
Contributors only; measured as stale counts in the three files (4 today, 0 after). Could break: nothing.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality - the catalogue's prose matches its tables
Before: probe - 4 stale count sites (hands.js:2, hands.test.ts:4, hands.rs:52-55, hands.rs:1280)
After: predicted 0 with the header-count test green
Method: probe for Before; the fix is comment-only and wants its S instrument first
Result: better
Gate: none
instrument: hands.test.ts: read SCRIPT's first doc line, map its count word to a number, assert it equals Object.keys of the FLAGS table (red today: nine vs 8).

title: An idle halo hide can race a new signal and hide the halo during a live phase
body:
## Summary
The idle hide checks the generation and then clears `shown` and hides as separate steps, so a non-idle signal landing between them sees `shown` still true, skips the show, and the halos go dark during a phase that wants them up.

## Description
apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/halo.rs:276-283: the timer thread loads the generation (`hide_still_due`), then `shown.store(false)` and `hide_all`. `signal` (halo.rs:260-271) bumps the generation and `shown.swap(true)`; if that swap runs between the timer's check and its store, it returns true, `show_all` is skipped, and the timer then hides every overlay. During listening the next 30 Hz level frame heals it within ~34 ms; during thinking or gate there may be no next frame until the phase changes. The window is microseconds wide. Fixed looks like: the check and the hide decided under one lock (a Mutex<(u64, bool)>), or the show path re-checking after a hide.

## Flow
- speech ends: idle signal, a hide is scheduled 4.5 s out
- 4.5 s later a gate card arrives as the timer fires; the timer has passed its generation check
- signal sees shown=true and returns; the timer stores false and hides: no halo while a card waits

## Expected impact
Ambient halo users at the moment a card lands exactly as an idle hide fires; measured as halos hidden while `wants_visible` (possible today, 0 after). Could break: nothing visible; a lock on a 30 Hz path.

## Evaluation
Claim: user - the halo is up whenever something is happening
Before: simulation - interleaving walked on halo.rs:260-283; not reproduced
After: predicted no hidden-while-wanted state
Method: simulation - reproducing needs controlled thread interleaving; a pure decision function would make it a unit test
Result: better
Gate: none
instrument: halo.rs: move show/hide bookkeeping into a pure `HaloState { generation, shown }` behind one Mutex with `on_signal(visible) -> ShowNow` and `on_timer(gen) -> HideNow`; a unit test drives timer-check, signal, timer-hide in that order and asserts the signal's show is not lost (red on today's two-atomic logic modelled the same way).
